      // Specify a pipe to compute the Internet checksum and return its identifier. This specification is subsequently converted
      // by our system into safe machine code. This code assumes that messages are always a multiple of four bytes long.
                                         
      int mk cksum pipe(struct pipel pl, reg t r)    f
          reg t reg;
          int pipe id;

           // This checksum works with 32 bits and is both commutative and non modifying (i.e., it does not alter its input).
          pipe lambda(pl, &pipe id, P GAUGE32, P COMMUTATIVE P NO MOD);       j
                 =
              reg p getreg(pl, pipe id, P VAR);           // Allocate an accumulate register (preserved across pipe applications)

             p input32(p inputr);                          // Get 32 bits of input from the pipe
             p cksum32(reg, p inputr);                     // Add input value to checksum accumulator
             p output32(p inputr);                         // Pass 32 bits of output to next pipe
          pipe end();
          =
           r reg;
          return pipe id;

         void simple remote write handler(void ash data, int nbytes)           f
                              
             int len; char dst;
                                                   
             if (!consume(&dst, sizeof(char ), NULL PIPE))      // Load destination address (first word)
                 return ASH ABORT;                              // Short message
             if (!consume(&len, sizeof(int), NULL PIPE))        // Load length (second word)
                 return ASH ABORT;                              // Short message
                         < +                   +
             if (nbytes len sizeof(int) sizeof(char ))         // Incomplete packet
                 return ASH ABORT;
             if (!consume(dst, len, NULL PIPE))             // Copy len bytes from (message buffer 8) to (dst).  +
                 return ASH ABORT;                          // Short or corrupt packet
             return ASH SUCCESS;                            // Success.

3.2 The abort protocol                                                              estimations of execution time are overly pessimistic, but simple to
                                                                                    implement:
When an ASH cannot complete execution it must abort. There
are many possible causes of an abort. First, external events (e.g.,
a device interrupt). Second, malicious or buggy ASH operations

For safety, the ASH system must guard against excessive execution                   its execution time estimation.
time, exceptions, and wild memory references and jumps in ASHs.

    Our TCP implementation allows ASHs to lower the cost of data

                                                                         9
5.3 Control transfer                                                                                         1500
Low-latency control transfer is also crucial to the performance of
                                                                                                                            user-level code
tightly-coupled distributed systems. Examples include remote lock
                                                                                                                            code using ASHs
allocation, reference counting, voting, global barriers, object loca-
tion queries, and method invocations. The need for low-latency




                                                                               Microseconds per round trip
remote computation is so overwhelming that the parallel commu-
nity has spawned a new paradigm of programming built around the
concept of active messages [43]: an efficient, unprotected transfer                                          1000
of control to the application in the interrupt handler.
     A key benefit of ASHs is that because the runtime of downloaded
code is bounded,they can be run in situations when performing a full
context switch to an unscheduled application is impractical. ASHs
thus allow applications to decouple latency-critical operations such
as message reply from process scheduling. Past systems precluded                                             500
protected, low-latency control transfer, or heavily relied on user-
level polling to achieve performance (e.g., in U-Net using signals
to indicate the arrival of a message instead of polling adds 30 mi-
croseconds to the 65-microsecond roundtrip latency [36]). The cost
of control transfers is sufficiently high that recently a dichotomy
has been drawn between control and data transfer in the interests of
constructing systems to efficiently perform just data transfer [39].                                           0
ASHs remove the restrictive cost of control transfer for those oper-                                                1   2      3      4       5   6       7   8
ations that can be expressed in terms of ASHs. We believe that the
                                                                                                                             Number of active processes
expressiveness of ASHs is sufficient for most operations subject to
low-latency requirements.
     As a simple experiment to illustrate the advantages of decou-             Figure 5: As the number of processes on the system increases, the
pling latency-critical operations from scheduling a process,we com-            cost of waiting for a process to be scheduled becomes increasingly
pare executing code in an in-kernel ASH versus in a user-level                 higher; times are in microseconds per roundtrip.
process while increasing the number of user processes. In the ex-
periment, the user-level processes are scheduled round-robin. As
shown in Figure 5, as the number of active processes increases,                UDP version does not set up and tear down connections. We have
the latency for the roundtrip remote increment increases, because              downloaded the UDP version into the kernel and run it as an ASH.
the scheduler is not integrated with the communication system,                 The TCP version has also been dynamically composed, but has only
